beliefs.practice: Use a single, long-lived Motor/Beanie client instance (shared across threads/requests) and avoid creating a new Mongo client per request; configure maxPoolSize to a sensible value (for example 100) rather than leaving an unbounded pool.

Never commit the cluster connection string or credentials to source control: read DOCUMENTDB_URI (and any username/password) from environment variables and/or store secrets in Azure Key Vault; provide only a .env.example with placeholders in the repo.

Choose a high-cardinality, evenly distributed partition key (Cosmos DB partition key) — not a skewed field like drug name — ideally use a hashed report_id or customer_id to avoid hot partitions and distribute traffic.

Use server-side schema validation (Beanie/Pydantic before insert and MongoDB schema validation rules where available) and reject or quarantine malformed records; store the original free-text in a raw_text field and the parsed fields as typed fields (drug, event, severity, onset_date as ISODate).

Create a compound index on the fields used by the aggregation (e.g., { drug: 1, event: 1 }) to support GROUP/COUNT aggregations efficiently rather than scanning full collection; create additional index on onset_date if queries filter by date.

For vector similarity search, store embedding vectors in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding: [float]) and create a vector index (HNSW/IVF) with explicit parameters (dimension, metric, M/efConstruction or indexType/metric params) tuned to your embedding size; avoid storing vectors in deeply nested fields.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors and 429 throttling responses; on 429, honor Retry-After if provided and back off rather than retrying immediately.

Use session-level consistency (or the account's configured Cosmos consistency) rather than attempting to emulate strong consistency in the app; avoid expecting immediate cross-region strong consistency for Mongo API unless account configuration guarantees it.

Avoid multi-document transactions where possible; design documents so updates are single-document atomic operations (embed related fields in one document) to improve performance and avoid the complexity of distributed transactions.
Use allowDiskUse:true for large aggregation pipelines that may exceed memory limits, and project/limit early in the pipeline to reduce intermediate document sizes and memory pressure.

When seeding or building large indexes, create indexes offline or during low-traffic windows and prefer background index builds if supported; for very large collections consider batching inserts rather than inserting one-by-one.

Don't log or persist raw PHI/PII in plaintext beyond what is necessary; if you must keep raw_text for auditing or re-parsing, protect it with access controls and consider encryption-at-rest and field-level encryption for sensitive fields.

Implement document TTL (a TTL index on an expiry field) for retention policies (e.g., automatically expire reports after retention period) rather than manual deletion scripts, to reduce operational overhead.

Instrument and monitor query performance and usage (OPCOUNTS, slow query logs, or the DocumentDB/MCP profiling tools) and create indexes only after identifying slow aggregation/lookup patterns with explain() plans.

Use bulk/batched writes (bulk_insert/insert_many) for seeding and high-throughput ingestion rather than single inserts to reduce round-trips and improve throughput; respect the cluster's RU/throughput limits when batching.

Protect the DocumentDB endpoint with network controls: restrict allowed client IPs, use VNet/private endpoints if available, and avoid exposing the cluster to the public internet without firewall rules.

When using LLM-driven extraction, treat the LLM output as untrusted: validate and canonicalize fields (normalize drug names, map severities to controlled vocabulary) and log parse confidence; quarantine ambiguous parses rather than writing invalid structured data.

Use appropriate writeConcern or durability settings for critical writes (e.g., w=majority) when available, but test behavior on the Cosmos Mongo API because some Mongo writeConcern options may be limited or behave differently under the Cosmos MongoDB compatibility layer.
